introduction: Choose a checked clock reading from Dan Robinson's original dashcam upload. Each button sets the path, warning and radar viewers to that historical time and selects the corresponding video position.
method: These are discrete clock observations, read from paused frames in the original upload. They are not a continuous synchronization of every frame. A video offset is recorded separately from the CDT clock printed on the footage, and CDT is converted to UTC by adding five hours. Browser seeking can land on a nearby frame. Compare the visible clock before making a precise comparison. No camera coordinates, viewing bearings, wind measurements or fatal impact locations are inferred from these samples.
coverage: On 2026-11-16 the whole upload was read for its edit. It runs as four passages, forward camera, rear camera, forward and forward again, with a fade in, a dissolve to the rear camera, a hard cut back to the forward camera, a jump in the caption clock and a fade out. No cut was found inside a passage. Between those boundaries every 15th frame was read, so a splice that removed less than about a second inside a passage would not show. No reuse credit was found, though a credit shorter than four seconds outside the caption box could fall between the sampled frames. Each passage has a clock reading at both ends, and every published sample sits on its passage's clock line within one second. Between the second and third forward passages the picture runs on without a cut while the caption jumps 11 s and the forward camera's own stamp keeps the same second, so the caption's basis changes there by 10 or 11 s. Against that stamp the caption runs 273 s behind in the first forward passage, 229 to 230 s behind after the cut and 219 s behind after the jump. If one forward camera keeping one clock recorded all three forward passages, the basis also moved 44 s at the cut, and this review did not test that. Which basis matches the true time is open, and the published samples read that caption, so their times carry the same question. The passages register the upload's edit and its caption clock. They place no camera and measure no bearing. The audio was not reviewed. Playing the original video still leaves the historical map paused, so frames between the samples do not acquire an invented event time.

guide.title: A video has two clocks
guide.text: Elapsed player time tells you where you are in an upload. The clock printed inside a shot may tell you when it happened. Cuts, replays and altered playback speed can break a single offset between the two. In Robinson's upload the caption clock advances about 0.98 s for every second of playback, and at the cut back to the forward camera it steps back 43 s, so some caption times appear twice. Here, each checked dashcam moment has its own correspondence. The intervening footage remains available to watch without claiming it is continuously synchronized.

guide.title: The camera is not the tornado
guide.text: A camera position describes the observer. A bearing describes where the camera points, not the distance to the visible feature. The El Reno Survey Project recommends recognizable landmarks, accurate clocks and location records because all three help register a view. Its guidance also warns that distortion from a wide angle lens complicates interpretation. A source photograph without that information remains valuable, but cannot establish a precise funnel location by itself.

sources.label: El Reno Survey Project field methods

guide.title: A visible edge is not a safe boundary
guide.text: Rain, spray and the viewing angle can obscure what the circulation is doing. In Robinson's sampled views, water on the windshield and low contrast hide much of the surrounding scene. A clear outline in one photograph does not establish the full width of damaging winds. The official path and documented damage must be read alongside the view.

guide.title: Damage rating and radar measurement
guide.text: The Enhanced Fujita scale estimates wind intensity from damage indicators and degrees of damage. Radar measurements describe sampled air motion with their own height, resolution and timing. They answer related questions with different evidence. This exhibit retains the final EF3 damage rating while discussing the mobile radar research separately. An old EF5 video title does not change the final rating.

sources.label: NWS explanation of the EF scale

guide.title: A landmark does not identify a person
guide.text: A road sign can help locate a camera. A matching vehicle shape is a lead, not a confirmed identity. Establishing a fatal impact requires more than a nearby timestamp or a recovery photograph. The remembrance map labels the kind of location the evidence supports and keeps unsupported coordinates out of the record.

guide.title: Bring the original record
guide.text: The most useful contribution is an original source with the relevant timestamp, visible landmarks and an explanation of the clock. Keep the camera operator's name and the upload version with the observation. A popular repost can remove those details. Research findings and disagreements belong beside the evidence, so a later correction can be traced.

reference_copy.video: VP9, 1920x1080, 30000/1001 frames per second, 26,017 frames, stream duration 868.100 s
reference_copy.use: Private reference copy for reading clocks and cuts. It is not committed, hosted or published, and no frame from it is republished.

shot_register.positions: Every position is the presentation time in seconds of one frame of the reference copy, as the container stores it in units of 1/16000 s, written to the millisecond. Its video stream lasts 868.100 s against the 868.161 s player duration. Each frame was decoded with ffmpeg as the first frame at or after the requested time.

clock_rate.method: Least squares slope of the caption clock against the player position, from caption OCR on every 15th frame (1,735 samples), after dropping samples more than 1.5 s off the fitted line. The three long passages give 0.98228, 0.98251 and 0.98312 clock seconds per player second, and the forward camera stamp gives 0.9826 over its first passage. The upload therefore shows about 0.98 s of clock time per second of playback.

cut_review.method: Scene scores from the ffmpeg scene filter over every frame, caption clock OCR and camera classification on every 15th frame, a contact sheet of every 120th frame, and frame by frame reading at every boundary those found. A transition runs from the last frame of the passage before it to the first frame of the passage after it, and the two fades run from the first frame and to the last frame of the upload. No reuse credit, title card or end card was found, though a credit shorter than four seconds outside the caption box could fall between the sampled frames. Audio was not reviewed.

transitions.note: The upload opens on black and fades in over about two seconds. The caption clock is legible but dim from 0.133 s, reading 6:16:58, then 6:16:59 from 0.634 s and 6:17:00 from 1.635 s.

The forward camera dissolves into the rear camera under the caption "Switch to rear-facing camera". A least squares mixture of the two pictures places the mixed frames from 353.153 s to 354.521 s. The caption clock reads 6:22:45 before and 6:22:46 after, so the edit presents the two cameras as simultaneous. That pairing rests on the caption alone, because the rear stamp was never set to the event date.

The rear camera at 6:27:15 cuts straight to the forward camera at 6:26:32. The caption clock steps back 43 s, so the next passage repeats storm time already shown from the rear. The caption "Front camera, starting before rear window blowout" follows.

The caption clock steps from 6:26:49 to 6:27:00 between consecutive frames. The forward picture runs on without a cut, and the forward camera stamp reads 18:30:39 on both sides, so the caption changes its basis by 11 s inside one camera passage.
Picture and caption fade to black from 867.100 s. The last legible label is 6:30:37 at 867.900 s, and black frames run from 867.934 s to the last frame at 868.067 s.

passages.note: Forward camera while driving, south on S Choctaw and then east on NW 10th/Reuter by the upload's own captions. The camera stamp runs 273 s ahead of the caption throughout. Anchors robinson-01, robinson-02 and robinson-03 lie here.

Rear camera through the rear window. Its yellow stamp at the top left is rotated half a turn, which suggests the picture was turned over in the edit, and it is dated 2012/07/23. The stamp keeps one offset from the caption, but its date shows it was never set for the event, so the caption is the only clock here. Anchors robinson-04 and robinson-05 lie here.
Forward camera again after the cut, with the vehicle on Reuter Road and the driver side inset from about 639.1 s. The camera stamp runs 229 to 230 s ahead of the caption, 44 s less than in forward-1.
The same forward picture after the caption step. The camera stamp runs 219 s ahead of the caption, 54 s less than in forward-1. Anchors robinson-06 and robinson-07 lie here.

shot_register.overlay_method: Caption edges are the first and last of every 15th frame on which a detector found the caption box. Captions fade in and out beyond them by up to about a second and a half. The inset edges are the first and last frames, half a second apart, on which it was seen by eye.
